source.title: Binary Sparse Coding for Interpretability
source.authors: Lucia Quirke; Stepan Shabalin; Nora Belrose

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Compares binary and continuous sparse coders and reports the effect of patching them on model loss, bearing on whether coder design changes reconstruction-related error. It does not analyze the structure or predictability of the residuals.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test linear predictability of SAE error, error-norm scaling, token overlap across SAE sizes, comparisons with random errors, or whether residual components encode distinct functions. Its relevant result is that binary coders incur a larger loss increase when patched than continuous coders. It does not directly establish that this difference is an artifact or that improved architectures reduce dark matter.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper proposing binary sparse coders. Its loss and FVU results compare its own coder against continuous TopK coders. It never measures the structure, predictability, scaling or functional role of SAE error, and it neither cites nor tests the dark-matter findings. A coder that increases error does not test whether dark matter is a training artifact (V6). Its idea that removed polysemanticity resurfaces elsewhere is only loosely related to V4, and it is a hypothesis about features, not about the error term.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors find that binarisation improves unweighted interpretability but increases FVU and patched loss. Continuous coders score slightly better once scores are frequency-weighted, because binary coders produce ultra-high-frequency uninterpretable features. They cannot recommend binary coders for most purposes. They take this negative result as support for polysemanticity being ineliminable. Binary coders do better on sparse probing after fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares binary and continuous sparse coders using patching-related loss and interpretability evaluations; it does not use the original study’s residual-predictability or cross-size error-context measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported patching-loss comparison varies layer and k; the paper’s broader experiments also vary coder type and model, but do not analyze residual structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Binarising TopK skip-transcoders and SAEs raises FVU and patched cross-entropy loss relative to continuous coders on SmolLM2-135M (Figure 1, Figures 14-17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining sparse-coder activations to binary values increases reconstruction error and patched loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Binary coders produce more ultra-high-frequency, uninterpretable features, one firing on over half of tokens (Figures 6-7). The authors hypothesise that information from low activation strengths is pushed into these features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemanticity removed from one part of a sparse code reappears elsewhere (in high-frequency features).

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-ablating bins of binary-transcoder features grouped by interpretability gives nearly equal loss increases, except for the two highest-interpretability bins (Figure 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature interpretability is largely unrelated to causal importance except at the extremes.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025, 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
record.problems: The patching-loss result is shown in a figure without exact values in the text. The comparison does not include random errors matched in size, and it does not characterize the residuals or identify whether coder training choices cause dark matter.

untested.parts: No regression of SAE error on input activations.
No per-token error-norm prediction, no cross-size context overlap, and no scaling of error with width. Width scaling is only mentioned as a limitation.
Patched loss is not compared with random errors of equal norm.
No decomposition of error into linear and nonlinear parts.
No circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term. The binned feature ablation in Figure 8 measures feature importance, not the error term.
No test of whether error comes from the sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents or the objective. KL fine-tuning is used only for sparse probing, and its effect on error structure is not reported.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 test and limits_scope label should be dropped: the rows are own-method comparisons, and no version is tested. The paper does not cite the dark-matter study. The 1.7B results (Table 2) are single-seed. The authors note that dead neurons and width could change their results.

versions.untested_parts: No analysis of whether SAE error is linearly predictable from input activations.
No per-token error-norm scaling or comparison of error contexts across SAE sizes.
Reports loss increases from patching coders, but does not compare reconstruction replacement with random errors of the same size.
No separation or characterization of linear and nonlinear error components.
No test of whether analyses of circuits or steering lose behavior when the error term is omitted.

Compares binary and continuous coders’ patching-related loss, but does not establish that dark matter mostly reflects training choices, test improved architectures or end-to-end training, or measure whether the residual itself shrinks.
